question: A buyer's associate threatens physical harm to a seller's family unless the seller signs a deed immediately, and the frightened seller signs. A contract or conveyance procured through this kind of unlawful threat, rather than genuine free will, is:
choice_a: Voidable at the option of the coerced party, due to duress
choice_b: Automatically ratified once signed, regardless of the threat
choice_c: Fully enforceable exactly as if freely negotiated
choice_d: Void only if the threat was made in writing
explanation: Duress -- coercion through an unlawful threat that overcomes a party's free will -- makes the resulting contract voidable at the coerced party's election, since genuine mutual assent (a required element of a valid contract) was never truly present.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.2 (mutual assent -- genuine assent) and general contract law principles

question: An elderly seller in declining health signs a sale contract at a steep discount after persistent, high-pressure demands from a caregiver who controls the seller's daily affairs and isolates the seller from family and independent advice. This contract is most likely voidable due to:
choice_a: Undue influence
choice_b: A valid arm's-length negotiation
explanation: Undue influence occurs when one party exploits a position of trust or dominance to overcome another's free will in a way that produces an unfair result -- distinct from ordinary persuasion, and grounds for voiding the resulting contract because genuine, voluntary assent was compromised.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.2 (mutual assent -- genuine assent) and general contract law principles

question: A seller innocently but incorrectly tells a buyer the roof was replaced two years ago, honestly believing this based on a prior owner's statement, when it was in fact never replaced. The buyer reasonably relies on this false statement of material fact in deciding to purchase. Because the seller had no intent to deceive, the buyer's remedy is most accurately described as a right to seek:
choice_a: Rescission for innocent (or negligent) misrepresentation, even absent the seller's fraudulent intent
choice_b: No remedy whatsoever, since only intentional fraud ever creates any remedy
choice_c: Automatic punitive damages against the seller
choice_d: Forced specific performance regardless of the misrepresentation
explanation: Innocent or negligent misrepresentation -- a false statement of material fact made without fraudulent intent -- can still support rescission of the contract, distinguishing it from fraud, which requires a knowing false statement made with intent to deceive and can additionally support a damages claim.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.2 (mutual assent) and V.D.5 (fraud and misrepresentation) distinctions, Pearson VUE #094401

question: Both the buyer and seller sign a contract referencing 'Lot 14,' each honestly but mistakenly believing Lot 14 includes a strip of land that, per the actual recorded plat, is really part of the adjoining Lot 15. Because both parties shared this identical erroneous belief about an essential fact central to the bargain, a court may grant:
choice_a: Rescission or reformation of the contract based on mutual mistake
choice_b: No remedy at all, since courts never address factual mistakes
choice_c: Rescission available only to the seller, never the buyer
choice_d: Automatic specific performance compelling the mistaken boundary description
explanation: When both parties share the same erroneous belief about a material fact fundamental to their bargain, courts may allow rescission (undoing the contract) or reformation (correcting the writing to reflect the parties' actual intent) under the doctrine of mutual mistake.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.2 (mutual assent -- genuine assent) and general contract law principles

question: A seller makes a math error calculating the asking price and lists a home for far less than intended, but the buyer has no reason to know of the mistake and accepts in good faith. Under the general rule governing this kind of one-sided (unilateral) mistake, the resulting contract is:
choice_a: Generally still enforceable against the mistaken party, since only one side was mistaken and the other reasonably relied on the terms as stated
choice_b: Automatically voidable at the mistaken seller's sole option, with no further inquiry
choice_c: Void from inception in every case involving any calculation error
choice_d: Unenforceable under the statute of frauds
explanation: Unlike mutual mistake, a unilateral mistake known only to one party generally does not excuse that party's performance unless the other party knew or should have known of the error, or enforcement would be unconscionable -- protecting a party who reasonably relied on the contract's stated terms.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.2 (mutual assent) and general contract law principles

question: A contract contains terms so one-sided and unfair, combined with such unequal bargaining power at formation, that enforcing it as written would shock the conscience of the court. A court may refuse to enforce all or part of such a contract under the doctrine of:
choice_a: Unconscionability
choice_b: Novation
explanation: Unconscionability allows a court to refuse enforcement (in whole or in part) of a contract or clause that is so one-sided or procedurally unfair -- often combined with grossly unequal bargaining power -- that enforcing it would be fundamentally unjust.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B (required elements of a valid contract) and general contract law principles

question: A standardized, pre-printed contract drafted entirely by one party (typically with greater bargaining power) and presented to the other party on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, with no realistic opportunity to negotiate its terms, is called a:
choice_a: Contract of adhesion
choice_b: Bilateral contract
explanation: A contract of adhesion is a standardized, non-negotiable agreement drafted by the stronger party; being adhesive in form does not automatically make it unenforceable, but courts scrutinize particular terms more closely for unconscionability given the lack of meaningful negotiation.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.A (types of contracts) and general contract law principles

question: A fully integrated, unambiguous written real estate contract generally cannot be contradicted by evidence of the parties' earlier oral or written negotiations that occurred before or at the same time as signing. This principle, which protects the finality of a completed written agreement, is called the:
choice_a: Parol evidence rule
choice_b: Statute of frauds
explanation: The parol evidence rule bars extrinsic evidence of prior or contemporaneous agreements from contradicting the terms of a final, fully integrated written contract, though it does not bar evidence of later modifications, fraud, or clarification of a genuine ambiguity.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance and interpretation) and general contract law principles

question: A written contract includes a clause stating: 'This agreement contains the entire understanding between the parties, superseding all prior negotiations, representations, or agreements not contained herein.' This clause, which is separate from the real-property doctrine describing what happens to contract terms at closing, is called a(n):
choice_a: Merger (integration) clause
choice_b: Acceleration clause
explanation: A merger (integration) clause signals that the written document is the final, complete expression of the parties' agreement, reinforcing the parol evidence rule's bar against outside prior or contemporaneous agreements -- distinct from the real-property 'merger doctrine' governing whether sales contract terms survive into the deed at closing.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance and interpretation) and general contract law principles

question: A contract provision states that the buyer's obligation to close does not arise unless and until the buyer's lender has issued final loan approval. Because the buyer's duty to perform depends on this event occurring first, the loan-approval requirement is a:
choice_a: Condition precedent
choice_b: Condition subsequent
explanation: A condition precedent is an event that must occur before a party's contractual duty to perform becomes absolute; here, the buyer has no obligation to close until the specified loan-approval condition is actually satisfied.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.4 (contingencies) and general contract law principles

question: At a real estate closing, the seller's delivery of the executed deed and the buyer's delivery of the purchase funds are ordinarily due to occur at the same time, with each party's performance excused only by the other's failure to tender its own performance. This mutual, simultaneous performance obligation illustrates:
choice_a: Concurrent conditions
choice_b: A condition subsequent
explanation: Concurrent conditions require both parties to be ready, willing, and able to perform at the same time -- neither buyer nor seller can sue for breach at closing without having tendered (or offered) their own performance first.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D (sales contract elements and closing performance) and general contract law principles

question: Two weeks before the scheduled closing date, a buyer sends the seller a written notice stating unequivocally that the buyer will not go through with the purchase under any circumstances. Even though the closing date has not yet arrived, the seller may immediately treat this clear, unequivocal statement as a present breach under the doctrine of:
choice_a: Anticipatory repudiation (anticipatory breach)
choice_b: Novation
explanation: Anticipatory repudiation allows the non-breaching party to treat a clear, unequivocal statement of future non-performance as an immediate breach, entitling that party to pursue remedies without waiting for the performance date to actually pass.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C.4 (breach of contract) and general contract law principles

question: A contractor completes a buyer's pre-closing repair obligation under the contract, but a minor, easily correctable defect remains -- such as a slightly miscolored paint touch-up -- that does not defeat the fundamental purpose of the repair. Under the doctrine of substantial performance, this minor deviation:
choice_a: Generally does not excuse the other party's obligation to perform, though the non-breaching party may recover damages for the minor defect
choice_b: Automatically excuses the other party from all further performance under the contract
choice_d: Constitutes a material breach entitling the buyer to rescind
explanation: Substantial performance -- completing the essential purpose of a contractual duty with only minor, non-material deviations -- generally does not excuse the other party's own performance, though the substantially performing party remains liable for damages caused by the minor deficiency.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance) and general contract law principles

question: A buyer under an executory purchase contract transfers the buyer's contractual right to purchase the property to a third party, without the buyer being personally discharged from the underlying obligations unless the contract or seller separately agrees otherwise. This transfer of contractual rights to a third party is called a(n):
choice_a: Assignment
choice_b: Novation
explanation: An assignment transfers a party's contractual rights (and sometimes delegates duties) to a third party, but unlike a novation, it does not automatically discharge the assignor from liability unless the other original party expressly releases them; many real estate contracts also include anti-assignment clauses restricting this right.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance) and general contract law principles

question: A buyer under a purchase contract, the seller, and a new substituted buyer all agree that the new buyer will step into the original buyer's exact contractual position, and the original buyer is fully and completely released from any further obligation under the contract. This three-party substitution, which fully discharges the original party, is called a:
choice_a: Novation
choice_b: Assignment
explanation: A novation requires the consent of all parties involved and results in the complete discharge and substitution of one contracting party for another -- distinct from a mere assignment, which transfers rights without necessarily releasing the original party from liability.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance) and general contract law principles

question: A buyer and a builder enter a new-construction contract that expressly grants a specific future homeowners association enforceable rights to certain warranty provisions, even though the association is not itself a signing party to the contract. That association is best described in contract law as a(n):
choice_a: Intended third-party beneficiary, who may enforce the contract's designated provisions despite not being an original contracting party
choice_b: Assignee, since only an assignee may ever enforce any contract term
choice_c: Party to the contract in every legal sense, identical to the buyer and builder
explanation: When a contract's parties intend to directly benefit a specific outside party, that party is an intended third-party beneficiary who may enforce the designated provisions, distinguishing it from an incidental beneficiary who merely happens to benefit without any enforceable right.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance) and general contract law principles

question: A seller who is owed an additional $2,000 by a buyer for a disputed post-closing repair agrees to accept $1,200 immediately in full and final settlement of the entire claim, and the buyer promptly pays that reduced amount. This settlement of a disputed claim through a substitute, mutually agreed performance is known as:
choice_a: Accord and satisfaction
choice_b: Liquidated damages
explanation: Accord and satisfaction occurs when parties to a disputed claim agree to a new, substitute performance (the accord) and that substitute performance is actually carried out (the satisfaction), fully discharging the original disputed obligation.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance) and general contract law principles

question: A property that is the subject of a pending sale contract is completely destroyed by fire through no fault of either party before closing, and the contract contains no controlling risk-of-loss provision. Under the common-law doctrine of impossibility of performance (or frustration of purpose), the parties' remaining contractual obligations may be:
choice_a: Discharged, since performance of the contract's fundamental purpose has become impossible through no fault of either party
choice_b: Automatically enforced exactly as written regardless of the destruction
choice_d: Reformed to require the seller to rebuild the destroyed structure
explanation: Impossibility of performance can discharge contractual duties when an unforeseen event destroys the subject matter essential to the contract's purpose through no fault of either party, though many states' equitable conversion rules or specific contract risk-of-loss clauses may allocate this risk differently in practice.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C.4 (breach, rescission, and termination) and general contract law principles

question: A contract requires written notice for any extension request, but a seller repeatedly accepts a buyer's informal, verbal extension requests without objection over the course of prior dealings. If the seller later attempts to strictly enforce the written-notice requirement without ever having signaled a change in that accepted practice, a court may find the seller has:
choice_a: Waived strict enforcement of that written-notice provision, at least as to the pattern of past instances
choice_b: Automatically voided the entire underlying contract
choice_d: Created a valid novation of the contract
explanation: Waiver is the voluntary and knowing relinquishment of a known contractual right, which can arise from a party's conduct (such as repeatedly accepting non-conforming performance) even without an express written waiver.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C (contract performance) and general contract law principles

question: A contract exchanges a valuable parcel of land for $10 and other valuable consideration, and a party later challenges the contract because the price paid was far below the land's fair market value. For purposes of contract validity, courts generally:
choice_a: Do not inquire into the adequacy (fairness) of the exchanged value, only whether legally sufficient consideration exists, absent fraud, duress, or unconscionability
choice_b: Automatically void any contract in which the price is below fair market value
choice_c: Require consideration to be exactly equal in value on both sides
choice_d: Treat inadequate consideration alone as automatic, conclusive proof of fraud
explanation: Courts generally examine only whether consideration is legally sufficient (something of legal value bargained for), not whether it is economically adequate or fair, leaving parties free to make even a bad bargain absent separate grounds like fraud, duress, or unconscionability.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.4 (lawful consideration) and general contract law principles

question: A contractor already contractually obligated to complete a specific repair by a certain date demands an extra $500 to finish on time, and the buyer reluctantly agrees. Under the pre-existing duty rule, the contractor's promise to do what the contractor was already legally obligated to do:
choice_a: Is not valid new consideration to support the additional $500 payment
choice_b: Is always valid new consideration, regardless of any pre-existing obligation
choice_c: Automatically creates a binding novation of the original contract
choice_d: Converts the original bilateral contract into a unilateral contract
explanation: Under the pre-existing duty rule, a promise to perform an act one is already legally obligated to perform does not constitute valid new consideration, meaning the additional promised payment may be unenforceable absent some genuinely new consideration or a recognized exception.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.4 (lawful consideration) and general contract law principles

question: A seller orally promises a longtime tenant that the tenant will be allowed to purchase the property at a fixed price once the seller decides to sell, with no signed writing of any kind. The tenant, reasonably relying on this promise, spends significant money on permanent improvements to the property. Even without a written, signed contract satisfying the statute of frauds, a court might enforce the seller's promise under the doctrine of:
choice_a: Promissory estoppel, based on the tenant's reasonable and detrimental reliance on the seller's promise
choice_b: The mailbox rule
explanation: Promissory estoppel can, in limited circumstances, allow enforcement of a promise the promisor should reasonably have expected to induce reliance, where the promisee did in fact reasonably and detrimentally rely on it, even absent traditional consideration or a writing.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.4 (lawful consideration) and general contract law principles

question: A property management agreement includes a clause attempting to relieve the broker of all liability for the broker's own negligence in managing the owner's property. This type of liability-limiting clause is called a(n):
choice_a: Exculpatory clause
choice_b: Acceleration clause
explanation: An exculpatory clause attempts to relieve a party of liability for its own negligence; courts frequently refuse to enforce such clauses where they attempt to excuse gross negligence, willful misconduct, or conduct violating public policy, such as a broker's fiduciary duties to a client.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.B.3 (property management agreement) and general contract law principles

question: A seller who has extended a purchase offer to a buyer decides, before the buyer has accepted, to withdraw the offer and clearly communicates that withdrawal to the buyer. This withdrawal of an offer before acceptance is called:
choice_a: Revocation, which terminates the offer and the offeree's power to accept it going forward
choice_b: A counteroffer
explanation: An offeror may generally revoke an ordinary offer at any time before acceptance, terminating the offeree's power to accept -- an important exception being an option contract, where the offeree has paid consideration for a period during which the offer cannot be revoked.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.1 (offer and counteroffer) and general contract law principles

question: A buyer's written purchase offer states no specific expiration date or deadline for acceptance. If the seller neither accepts nor rejects within a reasonable time under the circumstances, the offer:
choice_a: Lapses (automatically terminates) due to the passage of a reasonable time, even without an express deadline
choice_b: Remains open indefinitely until formally revoked
choice_c: Automatically converts into a binding counteroffer
explanation: An offer that does not specify a deadline lapses -- automatically terminates -- after a reasonable time has passed under the circumstances, since an offeree cannot be permitted to hold an offer open indefinitely by simply never responding.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.1 (offer and counteroffer) and general contract law principles

question: An offeree properly mails a signed written acceptance of an offer, but the offeror never actually receives that acceptance due to a postal error. Under the traditional common-law mailbox rule, that acceptance is generally treated as effective:
choice_a: The moment it is properly mailed (dispatched), not only once actually received by the offeror
choice_b: Only once actually received and read by the offeror
choice_c: Never, since a lost acceptance always defeats the resulting contract
choice_d: Only if hand-delivered rather than mailed
explanation: Under the traditional mailbox rule, a properly dispatched acceptance is effective upon mailing rather than receipt -- though the specific contract's terms, or a jurisdiction's variation, can modify this default rule, and the rule traditionally does not apply the same way to revocations, which are generally effective only upon receipt.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.1 (offer and counteroffer) and general contract law principles

question: A seller receives an unsolicited written purchase offer from a buyer and simply does not respond in any way -- no verbal acknowledgment, no signature, no conduct suggesting agreement. Under general contract law, this silence:
choice_a: Generally does not, by itself, constitute acceptance of the offer
choice_b: Always constitutes binding acceptance automatically after ten days
choice_c: Automatically creates an implied contract on the buyer's exact stated terms
choice_d: Converts the offer into an irrevocable option contract
explanation: Silence alone generally does not constitute acceptance of an offer as a matter of general contract law, though limited exceptions can arise from a prior course of dealing between the parties or the offeree's own conduct indicating assent.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.1 (offer and counteroffer) and general contract law principles

question: A residential contract sets earnest money at an amount so grossly disproportionate to the seller's foreseeable actual damages from a buyer's default that it appears designed purely to punish the buyer rather than reasonably estimate the seller's loss. A court reviewing such a clause may find it:
choice_a: An unenforceable penalty, since a valid liquidated damages clause must bear a reasonable relationship to anticipated actual damages at the time of contracting
choice_b: Automatically enforceable no matter how disproportionate the stated amount is
choice_c: Automatically converted into an award of punitive damages
choice_d: Legally irrelevant, since courts never review the reasonableness of a liquidated damages clause
explanation: A liquidated damages clause is enforceable only if it represents a reasonable estimate of anticipated actual damages made at the time of contracting; an amount so excessive that it functions as a punishment rather than compensation risks being struck down as an unenforceable penalty.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C.5 (liquidated, punitive, or compensatory damages) and IV.D.2 (earnest money and liquidated damages), Pearson VUE #094401

question: After closing, a buyer attempts to sue the seller for breaching a provision of the sales contract concerning the property's condition that was not repeated in, or expressly preserved to survive, the deed. Under the real-property doctrine of merger, once the deed is delivered and accepted at closing:
choice_a: Most sales contract provisions are generally considered merged into (superseded by) the deed, extinguishing the ability to sue on non-surviving contract terms unless the contract expressly provides that the provision survives closing
choice_b: Every provision of the sales contract automatically survives closing forever, regardless of the deed's terms
choice_c: The merger doctrine has no application whatsoever to real estate closings
choice_d: The deed becomes legally irrelevant once the underlying sales contract was signed
explanation: Under the doctrine of merger, most sales contract terms merge into, and are superseded by, the deed once it is delivered and accepted -- meaning a buyer generally cannot later sue on a non-surviving contract provision after closing -- though contracts commonly designate certain provisions (such as specific warranties or indemnities) to expressly survive closing.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.D.3 (equitable title and closing) and general real property contract-law principles

question: A Texas party seeking to sue for breach of a written real estate sales contract generally must file suit within:
choice_a: Four years from accrual of the cause of action, under the Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code's limitations provisions governing debt and contract actions
choice_b: Ninety days from the date of breach
choice_c: One year from the date of breach
choice_d: Ten years from the date of breach
explanation: Texas generally applies a four-year statute of limitations to suits for breach of a written contract, under the Civil Practice and Remedies Code's provisions governing debt and residual limitations periods -- meaning claims not brought within that window are typically time-barred regardless of their underlying merit.
source_note: Texas Civil Practice and Remedies Code Sections 16.004 and 16.051 (limitations periods)

question: An oral agreement for the sale of real property, though otherwise required to be in writing under the statute of frauds, may nonetheless be enforced in some cases if the buyer has taken possession, made substantial improvements, and paid all or part of the purchase price in clear reliance on the oral agreement. This equitable doctrine, allowing enforcement despite the missing writing, is known as the:
choice_a: Partial performance exception to the statute of frauds
choice_b: Parol evidence rule
explanation: The partial performance exception allows courts, in equity, to enforce an otherwise unenforceable oral real estate agreement when a party's conduct -- such as taking possession, making improvements, and paying some or all of the price -- makes it clear a genuine agreement existed and would work an injustice to leave unenforced.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.C.6-7 (Statute of Frauds) and general contract law principles

question: A person who has been formally adjudicated by a court to be mentally incompetent, with a court-appointed guardian, generally lacks the legal capacity to enter a binding real estate contract. Such a contract, entered into after that judicial adjudication, is typically treated as:
choice_a: Void, rather than merely voidable, because the person has been judicially declared to lack contractual capacity entirely
choice_b: Fully enforceable exactly as with any other competent adult
choice_c: Voidable only at the guardian's election, and only within one year
choice_d: Automatically ratified upon the incompetent person's death
explanation: A contract entered into by a person already judicially adjudicated incompetent is generally treated as void, since that person has no legal capacity to contract at all -- a stricter outcome than the voidable status typically given to a minor's contract, where legal capacity exists but is simply limited by age.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.B.3 (legally competent parties) and IV.C.2-3 (void vs. voidable), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A real estate broker retained to sell one specific listed property, with authority limited to that particular transaction rather than ongoing authority to bind the principal generally, is classified in agency law as a:
choice_a: Special agent
choice_b: General agent
explanation: A special agent's authority is limited to a specific act or transaction -- the typical role of a listing or buyer's broker -- distinguishing it from a general agent (ongoing authority across a defined range of matters, such as a property manager) or a universal agent (broad authority across virtually all of a principal's affairs).
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E (types of agency) and general agency law principles

question: An individual is granted an extremely broad power of attorney authorizing them to handle virtually all of a principal's legal and business affairs, without limitation to a particular transaction or category of matters. That individual is acting as a(n):
choice_a: Universal agent
choice_b: Special agent
explanation: A universal agent holds the broadest possible grant of authority, typically covering nearly all of the principal's affairs, in contrast to a special agent (limited to a specific transaction) or a general agent (limited to a defined category of ongoing matters).
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E (types of agency) and general agency law principles

question: A principal never actually grants an agent authority to make a particular representation, but the principal's own words or conduct lead a reasonable third party to believe the agent has that authority, and the third party justifiably relies on it. The principal may be bound to the third party under the doctrine of:
choice_a: Apparent (ostensible) authority, even though the agent lacked actual authority to act
choice_b: Actual express authority only
choice_d: No doctrine binds the principal under these facts
explanation: Apparent authority arises from the principal's own manifestations to a third party -- not from any communication to the agent -- and can bind the principal to a reasonable, justifiably relying third party even where the agent lacked actual (express or implied) authority.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E-F (agency relationships) and general agency law principles

question: An agent enters into an agreement that exceeds the scope of the agent's actual authority, but the principal later learns the agreement's full terms and voluntarily accepts its benefits, thereby retroactively approving the agent's originally unauthorized act. This retroactive approval is called:
choice_a: Ratification
choice_b: Estoppel
explanation: Ratification occurs when a principal, with full knowledge of the material facts, retroactively approves an agent's originally unauthorized act, effectively treating it as if the agent had actual authority all along.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.F (creation and termination of agency) and general agency law principles

question: A principal knowingly allows a person to repeatedly appear to third parties as the principal's agent, without ever correcting that impression, and a third party reasonably and detrimentally relies on the appearance of that agency relationship. The principal may later be prevented from denying the agency relationship existed, under the doctrine of:
choice_a: Agency by estoppel
choice_b: Ratification
explanation: Agency by estoppel prevents a principal from later denying an agency relationship existed where the principal's own failure to correct a known, ongoing misimpression caused a third party to reasonably and detrimentally rely on the appearance of that relationship.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E-F (agency relationships) and general agency law principles

question: An agent is given authority to sell a property specifically in order to satisfy a debt the principal separately owes to that same agent, meaning the agent holds an actual property interest in the subject matter of the agency itself, not merely a role representing the principal. This special category of agency, which the principal generally cannot revoke at will, is called:
choice_a: Agency coupled with an interest
choice_b: Subagency
explanation: Agency coupled with an interest arises when the agent has an actual property interest in the subject matter of the agency (beyond ordinary compensation), which generally makes the agency irrevocable by the principal alone, unlike an ordinary agency that either party may typically terminate.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.F (creation and termination of agency) and general agency law principles

question: Under the traditional (pre-modern buyer-agency) MLS cooperation model, a cooperating broker who shows a listed property to a prospective buyer, without any separate buyer representation agreement in place, may historically have been acting as a:
choice_a: Subagent of the listing broker, owing fiduciary duties to the seller rather than to the buyer being shown the property
choice_b: Agent of the buyer exclusively, owing no duty at all to the seller
explanation: Under the older subagency model, a cooperating broker showing an MLS-listed property without a buyer representation agreement was often legally a subagent of the listing broker, meaning fiduciary duties actually ran to the seller -- a source of significant buyer confusion that helped drive the industry's shift toward express buyer representation and, in Texas, intermediary practice.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E (types of agency -- subagency) and V.B.1.d (multiple listing service), Pearson VUE #094401

question: An investor instructs an agent to purchase a parcel of land without revealing to the seller that the agent is acting on the investor's behalf, so the seller reasonably believes the agent is buying for themself. Once the seller later learns of the investor's existence, that investor is generally:
choice_a: Bound by, and generally able to enforce, the contract the agent made on the investor's behalf as an undisclosed principal, subject to certain limitations
choice_b: Never bound by any contract entered into without disclosing the principal's identity
choice_c: Automatically relieved of all liability under the contract because the seller was misled about the buyer's identity
choice_d: Treated in every respect as a universal agent
explanation: Under the undisclosed principal doctrine, a principal whose existence and identity were concealed from the third party at contracting is generally still bound by, and may generally enforce, the contract the agent made -- subject to certain limitations, such as defenses the third party could have raised against the agent personally.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E (types of agency) and general agency law principles

question: Beyond the agent's fiduciary duties running to the principal, agency law also recognizes reciprocal duties running from the principal to the agent. These typically include the principal's duty to:
choice_a: Compensate the agent as agreed, reimburse authorized expenses, and cooperate so the agent can perform the agency
choice_b: Owe no duties whatsoever, since fiduciary duties run in only one direction under agency law
choice_c: Personally supervise the agent's every action moment-to-moment
choice_d: Indemnify the agent against every conceivable loss, regardless of the agent's own fault
explanation: Agency law imposes reciprocal duties on the principal, including compensating the agent as agreed, reimbursing the agent for authorized expenses incurred in performing the agency, and cooperating with the agent so the agency's purpose can actually be carried out.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.E-G (agency relationships and obligations) and general agency law principles

question: A broker who materially breaches a fiduciary duty owed to the broker's own client -- such as secretly holding an undisclosed adverse interest in the same transaction -- risks which consequence regarding the broker's earned compensation for that transaction?
choice_a: Forfeiture of the broker's right to a commission, even if the client cannot separately prove additional monetary damages
choice_b: No consequence at all to the broker's commission under any circumstance
choice_c: An automatic doubling of the broker's commission as a statutory penalty against the client
choice_d: Automatic conversion of the listing into a net listing
explanation: A broker's material breach of fiduciary duty can independently forfeit the broker's right to compensation for that transaction -- a remedy available even where the client cannot prove additional consequential damages, since the breach itself undermines the very basis for earning the commission.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.G (licensee obligations) and general agency law principles

question: Beyond completion of purpose, mutual agreement, expiration of term, or death/incapacity of a party, an agency relationship may also automatically terminate by operation of law upon:
choice_a: Destruction of the subject property or the principal's bankruptcy, either of which can make continuation of the agency impossible or unlawful
choice_b: The agent taking a scheduled vacation
choice_d: A temporary decline in local market conditions
explanation: Agency relationships can also terminate by operation of law upon events such as destruction of the property that is the subject of the agency, or the principal's bankruptcy, either of which can render the agency's purpose impossible or unlawful to continue.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.F (creation and termination of agency), Pearson VUE #094401

question: In general agency law as applied to real estate brokerage, the term 'customer' (as distinguished from 'client') refers to:
choice_a: A party to a transaction to whom the licensee owes basic honesty and fair dealing, but not the full fiduciary duties owed to the licensee's actual represented client
choice_b: Any party who has signed a listing or buyer representation agreement with the broker
choice_c: A synonym for 'client,' with no legal distinction between the two terms
choice_d: Only a party who has already closed on a prior transaction with the broker
explanation: In agency terminology, a 'client' is the party the licensee actually represents and to whom the full fiduciary duties are owed, while a 'customer' is an unrepresented party to the same transaction who is nonetheless owed baseline honesty and fair dealing -- an important distinction for understanding the scope of an agent's obligations.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline IV.G (licensee obligations to parties of a transaction) and general agency law principles

question: A homeowner refinances an existing mortgage on their principal residence with a new lender, creating a new security interest in the home. Under the Truth in Lending Act's right of rescission, the homeowner generally has how long after the transaction to cancel, absent a request to waive that period for a bona fide personal financial emergency?
choice_a: Three business days
choice_b: Thirty calendar days
explanation: TILA's right of rescission generally gives a consumer three business days to cancel most transactions creating a new security interest in their principal dwelling, such as many refinances and home equity loans -- but this right does NOT apply to a purchase-money mortgage used to acquire or build the home in the first place, since Congress did not want to jeopardize a seller's ability to complete a sale.
source_note: 15 U.S.C. Section 1635; Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.23, verified via consumerfinance.gov

question: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits credit discrimination based on several factors that are not explicitly enumerated as protected classes under the Fair Housing Act itself, most notably including:
choice_a: Marital status and age, provided the applicant has the legal capacity to contract
choice_b: Race and color exclusively, simply duplicating the Fair Housing Act's protections with no additions
explanation: ECOA's prohibited bases include race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (for applicants with contractual capacity), receipt of public assistance income, and the exercise of rights under the Consumer Credit Protection Act -- notably adding marital status and age, categories the Fair Housing Act does not explicitly protect in the housing-transaction context itself.
source_note: Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. Section 1691(a); Regulation B

question: A lender denies a borrower's completed mortgage loan application. Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's Regulation B, the lender must notify the applicant of the adverse action taken, and provide (or offer to provide upon timely request) the specific reasons for the denial, within:
choice_a: 30 days of receiving the completed application
choice_b: 3 business days
choice_d: There is no federal notification requirement of any kind
explanation: Regulation B requires a creditor to notify an applicant of action taken on a completed application, including any adverse action, within 30 days, and to provide (or offer, upon a timely request) a statement of the specific reasons for the denial.
source_note: Regulation B (ECOA), 12 CFR 1002.9(a)(1), verified via consumerfinance.gov

question: A home seller, as a condition of the sale, requires the buyer to purchase title insurance from a specific title company chosen by the seller. This practice is most directly restricted by:
choice_a: RESPA Section 9, which generally prohibits a seller from requiring the buyer, as a condition of sale, to use a particular title insurance company
choice_b: The Fair Housing Act
choice_d: No federal law addresses this practice
explanation: RESPA Section 9 -- separate from Section 8's prohibition on referral kickbacks -- specifically bars a seller from conditioning a sale on the buyer's use of a particular title insurance company, protecting the buyer's ability to independently shop for title and closing services.
source_note: Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act Section 9, 12 U.S.C. Section 2608
